summary: The classic hand game starts with just three legal gestures.
source_basis: Rock paper scissors uses three standard gestures.

summary: Standard DNA is written with a four-letter molecular alphabet.
source_basis: Canonical DNA uses four nucleobases.

summary: One human hand usually supplies the first intuitive five-count.
source_basis: A typical human hand has five fingers.

summary: A standard die has six equally likely faces.
source_basis: A standard cubic die has six faces.

summary: The basic civil week is a seven-day repeating cycle.
source_basis: The standard civil week has seven days.

summary: The modern Solar System count stops at eight recognized planets.
source_basis: The Solar System has eight planets.

summary: A dozen is one of the most common everyday counting bundles.
source_basis: A dozen is defined as exactly twelve.

summary: The standard civil year is split into twelve named months.
source_basis: The Gregorian calendar year has twelve months.

summary: A full civil day is traditionally divided into twenty-four hours.
source_basis: The modern day is divided into twenty-four hours.

summary: Modern English writing works with twenty-six basic letters.
source_basis: The English alphabet has twenty-six letters.

canonical_name: Chess pieces at the start of a game
summary: A chess game opens with thirty-two pieces on the board.
source_basis: Standard chess starts with sixteen pieces per side.

summary: A standard deck compresses four suits into fifty-two distinct cards.
source_basis: A standard deck contains fifty-two cards.

summary: Triplets over a four-letter DNA alphabet yield sixty-four codons.
source_basis: The genetic code is built from triplets over four nucleotide symbols.

summary: The modern full-size piano keyboard has eighty-eight keys.
source_basis: A modern full-size piano has eighty-eight keys.

canonical_name: Bones in an adult human body
summary: An adult human skeleton contains just over two hundred bones.
source_basis: The typical adult human skeleton contains 206 bones.

summary: A common civil year contains three hundred sixty-five days.
source_basis: A common Gregorian year has 365 days.

canonical_name: Somatic cells in an adult C. elegans
summary: The famous model nematode is small enough that its adult somatic cell count is fixed and countable.
source_basis: Adult hermaphrodite C. elegans has 959 somatic cells.

canonical_name: Naked-eye stars across the whole sky
summary: Even under dark skies, the unaided eye only gets access to a few thousand stars.
source_basis: Roughly six thousand stars are visible to the naked eye over the whole celestial sphere.

canonical_name: Base pairs in the human mitochondrial genome
summary: Human mitochondrial DNA is tiny compared with the nuclear genome but still spans over sixteen thousand base pairs.
source_basis: The human mitochondrial genome has 16,569 base pairs.

summary: The human genome contains only on the order of twenty thousand protein-coding genes.
source_basis: The human genome has about twenty thousand protein-coding genes.

canonical_name: Words in the King James Bible
summary: A single classic religious text already contains hundreds of thousands of words.
source_basis: The King James Bible contains 783,137 words.

summary: A single 1080p image already contains a bit over two million pixels.
source_basis: Full HD uses a 1920 by 1080 pixel raster.

summary: Even the tiny 2x2 cube already has millions of reachable states.
source_basis: The Pocket Cube has 3,674,160 reachable positions.

canonical_name: Base pairs in the E. coli genome
summary: A common bacterium already carries several million base pairs of DNA.
source_basis: The Escherichia coli K-12 genome has 4,641,652 base pairs.

canonical_name: Base pairs in the yeast genome
summary: Baker's yeast jumps into the tens of millions of base pairs.
source_basis: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome contains about 12,157,105 base pairs.

summary: A single 8K image pushes into the tens of millions of pixels.
source_basis: 8K UHD uses a 7680 by 4320 pixel raster.

canonical_name: Base pairs in the human genome
summary: The haploid human genome contains about 3.2 billion base pairs.
source_basis: The haploid human genome is about 3.2 billion base pairs long.

summary: The entire IPv4 internet only has a few billion possible addresses.
source_basis: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long.

summary: The current human population is a bit over eight billion people.
source_basis: UN population materials place the world population at roughly 8.2 billion.

summary: YouTube says more than twenty billion videos have been uploaded to the platform.
source_basis: YouTube reported that over 20 billion videos had been uploaded as it turned twenty.

summary: The human brain contains on the order of eighty-six billion neurons.
source_basis: A common estimate for the human brain is about 86 billion neurons.

summary: Our galaxy contains roughly one hundred billion stars.
source_basis: The Milky Way is commonly estimated to contain about 100 billion stars.

summary: The sliding 15-puzzle already has over ten trillion reachable states.
source_basis: The 15-puzzle has 16!/2 reachable configurations.

summary: A human body contains on the order of tens of trillions of cells.
source_basis: A widely cited estimate puts the human body at about 37.2 trillion cells.

summary: The gut microbiome alone contains tens of trillions of bacterial cells.
source_basis: A common estimate gives the human body about 38 trillion bacterial cells.

summary: Brain connectivity climbs to roughly one hundred trillion synapses.
source_basis: The human brain is commonly estimated to contain about 100 trillion synapses.

summary: A 48-bit hardware address space already covers hundreds of trillions of identifiers.
source_basis: Standard MAC addresses are 48 bits long.

summary: DES is historically important partly because its 56-bit key space became brute-forceable.
source_basis: DES uses a 56-bit effective key length.

summary: A 60-bit brute-force search already means more than one quintillion candidate keys.
source_basis: A 60-bit symmetric key has 2^60 possible values.

summary: A full 64-bit value space spans about 18 quintillion possibilities.
source_basis: A 64-bit pattern has 2^64 distinct values.

summary: The ordinary 3x3 Rubik's Cube has over forty-three quintillion reachable positions.
source_basis: The 3x3 Rubik's Cube has 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 reachable positions.

canonical_name: Molecules in a drop of water
summary: Even a tiny drop of water contains around a sextillion molecules.
source_value_text: 0.05 mL drop x 1 g/mL x N_A / 18.01528 g/mol
source_basis: Derived from a representative 0.05 mL drop of water, water density, and the molar mass of water.
derivation_note: count = volume x density / molar_mass x Avogadro_constant

qualifiers.measurement: molecules in a representative water drop

summary: A standard Sudoku already allows sextillions of completed grids.
source_basis: The number of valid completed 9x9 Sudoku solution grids is 6,670,903,752,021,072,936,960.

summary: The observable universe is estimated to contain around two sextillion stars.
source_basis: A common order-of-magnitude estimate for stars in the observable universe is about two sextillion.

summary: By definition, 12 grams of carbon-12 contains one mole of atoms.
source_basis: One mole equals Avogadro's number of entities.

canonical_name: Human body cells across all living humans
summary: Multiplying one human body's cells by all living humans produces a count in the hundreds of sextillions.
source_basis: Derived from UN-scale world population and a representative 37.2 trillion cells per human body.

canonical_name: Molecules in one liter of water
summary: A liter of water contains on the order of ten septillion molecules.
source_basis: Derived from one liter of water at about one kilogram mass, water's molar mass, and Avogadro's constant.

summary: A human body contains roughly ten octillion atoms.
source_basis: A common order-of-magnitude estimate for atoms in a human body is around 7 x 10^27.

summary: A DNA strand only fifty bases long already spans around 10^30 possible sequences.
source_basis: Each of 50 positions can take one of four DNA bases.

summary: UUIDv4 has 122 random bits, giving a huge but standardized identifier space.
source_basis: UUID version 4 carries 122 random bits after fixed version and variant fields.

summary: IPv6 expands the internet address space to about 3.4 x 10^38 possibilities.
source_basis: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long.

summary: Earth's atmosphere contains on the order of 10^44 molecules.
source_basis: Estimated from total atmospheric mass, mean molar mass of air, and Avogadro's constant.

summary: The number of legal chess positions is estimated in the tens of quattuordecillion.
source_basis: A standard estimate places the number of legal chess positions around 4.82 x 10^44.

summary: SHA-1's 160-bit output space contains about 10^48 possible digests.
source_basis: SHA-1 produces 160-bit hash outputs.

summary: Eighty DNA bases already define a sequence space larger than 10^48.
source_basis: Each of 80 positions can take one of four DNA bases.

summary: Earth contains about 10^50 atoms, making planetary matter feel less abstract.
source_basis: Order-of-magnitude atom count from Earth mass and average nucleon mass.

summary: A 90-base oligonucleotide already spans an immense search space.
source_basis: Each position in a DNA string can be A, C, G, or T.

summary: Jupiter's mass corresponds to roughly 10^54 atoms, many orders above Earth-like scales.
source_basis: Order-of-magnitude atom count from Jupiter mass and hydrogen-dominated composition.

summary: The Sun contains about 10^57 nucleons, a useful stellar particle-count anchor.
source_basis: Estimated by dividing solar mass by proton mass.

summary: AES-192 has a standardized 192-bit key space used in modern cryptography.
source_basis: AES-192 uses 192-bit keys.

summary: At 100 bases, DNA sequence space rises to around 10^60 possibilities.
source_basis: Each position in a DNA string can be A, C, G, or T.

summary: A shuffled deck has so many possible orders that almost every real shuffle has likely never occurred before.
source_basis: A deck ordering is a permutation of 52 distinct cards.

summary: Converting the Milky Way's baryonic mass into nucleons gives a count around 10^68.
source_basis: Order-of-magnitude conversion from Milky Way baryonic mass to nucleon count.

summary: At 120 bases, sequence space reaches the rough scale of 10^72 possibilities.
source_basis: Each position in a DNA string can be A, C, G, or T.

summary: A 256-bit hash output space contains about 10^77 possible digests.
source_basis: SHA-256 produces 256-bit outputs.

summary: Ed25519 uses a private-key space on the order of 2^252, central to modern signatures.
source_basis: Ed25519's subgroup order is close to 2^252.

summary: A classic rough estimate puts the observable universe near 10^80 atoms.
source_basis: A standard order-of-magnitude estimate for atoms in the observable universe is about 10^80.

canonical_name: CMB photons in the observable universe
summary: The cosmic microwave background contributes around 10^89 photons to the observable universe.
source_basis: Common cosmology order-of-magnitude estimate for total CMB photons.

canonical_name: Total particles in the observable universe
summary: Including photons, neutrinos, and baryons gives a rough total near 10^90 particles.
source_basis: Order-of-magnitude aggregate from standard cosmological particle-population estimates.

summary: Even a short protein length of 80 residues spans a sequence space near 10^104.
source_basis: Each residue position can take one of twenty standard amino acids.

summary: At 90 residues, protein sequence space climbs past 10^117 possibilities.
source_basis: Each residue position can take one of twenty standard amino acids.

summary: Claude Shannon's famous estimate for possible chess games is about 10^120.
source_basis: The Shannon number estimates the game-tree complexity of chess at about 10^120.

summary: SHA-384 expands digest space to roughly 10^115 possibilities.
source_basis: SHA-384 produces 384-bit outputs.

canonical_name: Planck areas on the observable-universe boundary
summary: Dividing the observable-universe boundary area by Planck area gives a count near 10^123.
source_basis: Derived using observable-universe boundary area and Planck length.

summary: Earth's volume corresponds to about 10^125 Planck-volume cells.
source_basis: Derived from Earth's volume and Planck length.

summary: The Sun's volume corresponds to about 10^131 Planck-volume cells.
source_basis: Derived from solar volume and Planck length.

summary: A modest 100-amino-acid protein already lives in an unimaginably large sequence space.
source_basis: Each of 100 positions can take one of twenty standard amino acids.

summary: At 110 residues, protein sequence space is around 10^143 possibilities.
source_basis: Each residue position can take one of twenty standard amino acids.

summary: A 512-bit hash output space is already around 10^154 possibilities.
source_basis: SHA-512 produces 512-bit outputs.

summary: The P-521 elliptic-curve private-key space is on the order of 2^521, near 10^157.
source_basis: P-521 uses roughly a 521-bit private scalar range.

summary: A 120-residue protein spans about 10^156 possible sequences.
source_basis: Each residue position can take one of twenty standard amino acids.

summary: A 266-base DNA sequence space sits near 10^160 possibilities.
source_basis: Each position in a DNA string can be A, C, G, or T.

summary: The game of Go explodes into an estimated 2.08 x 10^170 legal positions.
source_basis: A commonly cited estimate puts the number of legal Go positions at about 2.08 x 10^170.
